analysis.one_liner: Terminates the Treasury's remaining TARP bailout authority immediately.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote in the House Financial Services Committee, and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ended the Treasury Secretary's authority under the Troubled Asset Relief Program — the 2008 bank bailout — right away. It would also bar Treasury from spending anything on promises it had already made but not yet funded, including housing and foreclosure-relief assistance under the bailout law. The bill went to the House Financial Services Committee and never went any further.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, in the sense that no further bailout money could be committed or spent under TARP, ending the program's remaining exposure. But the same provision would have cut off money for homeowners still counting on foreclosure-prevention help funded through TARP.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers opposed to further bailout spending

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the 2008 bailout law to terminate the Treasury Secretary's TARP authority, ending any ability to make new asset purchases or commitments under the program.
It would bar Treasury from spending money on any already-made but unfunded commitment to purchase, closing off further use of unspent bailout funds.

By late 2010 the program's original purchase authority was already scheduled to lapse on its own on October 3, 2010, so the practical effect of the bill was mainly to freeze remaining unspent commitments rather than stop a new wave of bailouts.

analysis.who_pays: Homeowners relying on TARP-funded foreclosure-relief programs: the bill explicitly blocks spending on housing assistance commitments made under the bailout law. Banks and other institutions expecting any remaining disbursements would also lose access.

drawbacks.text: The bill specifically prohibits spending on housing assistance commitments under sections 109 and 110 of the bailout law, which funded mortgage-modification and foreclosure-prevention help — so ending TARP would have pulled support out from under struggling homeowners mid-crisis.

Ending the program's authority immediately, rather than letting unfunded commitments run out naturally, could have left the government unable to honor promises already made, creating uncertainty for institutions and homeowners depending on them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — permanently ending bailout authority — was largely symbolic by late 2010, since the bailout law's own purchase authority was set to expire on October 3, 2010 anyway. The real substance was the provision freezing unfunded commitments, and that cut both ways: it protected taxpayers from further bailout spending but would have taken money away from homeowners getting foreclosure help. An honest supporter had to accept that the bill rescued taxpayers at the expense of struggling borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Erik Paulsen introduced the bill on September 28, 2010 — five days before TARP's own purchase authority was set to lapse.
It attracted no cosponsors at all.
The House Financial Services Committee took no action after the referral; there is no record of a hearing, markup, or committee vote, and the bill never reached the House floor.
The bill expired with the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo prevailed, which mattered most for homeowners in TARP-funded mortgage-relief programs, who kept their assistance, and for the Treasury, which retained authority over remaining commitments. Banks awaiting any leftover disbursements also kept their place in line, though TARP's main spending power was expiring within days regardless.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Homeowners in mortgage-relief programs kept funding

for.name: Rep. Erik Paulsen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to terminate TARP authority on September 28, 2010.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Barney Frank (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or committee vote after referring it.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote and no cosponsor from either party, so the record shows only a single Republican sponsor and no organized opposition or support.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently cut off any further bailout disbursements to financial institutions, but by late 2010 most bank aid under TARP had already been extended and repaid, so the practical loss was small. Institutions and Treasury-related housing programs would have lost access to unspent, already-committed funds.

The bill bars spending on housing assistance commitments made under sections 109 and 110 of the bailout law, which funded homeowner assistance. Ending that flow would have reduced help for homeowners facing foreclosure.
